Decayed
də-kād'
v. and adj. (fallen away, wasted; used of a builder's strength and of ruined places God promises to raise)
Old French decair, from Latin de-, down, and cadere, to fall — a falling away by degrees rather than at a stroke.

Biblical Definition

The word appears at the hardest moment of Nehemiah's work and in the sweetest promise of Isaiah. On the wall: “And Judah said, The strength of the bearers of burdens is decayed, and there is much rubbish; so that we are not able to build the wall” (Neh 4:10). Three things are named — failing strength, too much rubble, and a conclusion drawn from them. It is the conclusion that is fatal, and it comes from within the workforce, not from Sanballat. Nehemiah's answer in the following verses is to set the people by families with a weapon in one hand, and the wall was finished in fifty and two days. Against this stands Isaiah's word about the God who reverses decay: “That confirmeth the word of his servant, and performeth the counsel of his messengers; that saith to Jerusalem, Thou shalt be inhabited; and to the cities of Judah, Ye shall be built, and I will raise up the decayed places thereof” (Isa 44:26). And Paul says the same of the body a Christian is living in: “though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day” (2Co 4:16).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines decay as a gradual failure of health, strength, soundness or prosperity; a falling into a worse state; and to decay as to pass from a state of soundness gradually to a worse.

expand to see more

DECAY, v.i. [L. de and cado, to fall.] To pass gradually from a sound, prosperous, or perfect state, to a less perfect state, or towards weakness or dissolution.

2. To fail; to decline; to be gradually impaired.

DECAY, n. Gradual failure of health, strength, soundness, prosperity, or of any species of excellence or perfection.

The strength of the bearers of burdens is decayed. Neh. iv.

Key Scripture

Neh 4:10 — "And Judah said, The strength of the bearers of burdens is decayed, and there is much rubbish; so that we are not able to build the wall."

Neh 4:6 — "So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work."

Isa 44:26 — "That confirmeth the word of his servant, and performeth the counsel of his messengers; that saith to Jerusalem, Thou shalt be inhabited; and to the cities of Judah, Ye shall be built, and I will raise up the decayed places thereof:"

2Co 4:16 — "For which cause we faint not; but though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day."

Modern Corruption

Nehemiah 4:10 is quoted as a description of burnout, when the verse's sting is not the tiredness but the sentence drawn from it — we are not able.

expand to see more

Everything Judah says in Nehemiah 4:10 is factually true. The bearers of burdens were exhausted; there was a great deal of rubbish; the wall was half built and the enemy was massing. Scripture does not rebuke the report, and it is a mistake to preach this verse as though weariness were sin — four verses earlier the same people had a mind to work, and the Lord Jesus Himself sat down at a well being wearied with His journey. The failure is in the last clause: so that we are not able to build the wall. A true account of the strength has been turned into a verdict about the outcome, and the verdict leaves God out. That is the point at which honest tiredness becomes unbelief, and it is a very short step, taken quietly, usually by the most diligent workers rather than the idle ones.

Nehemiah's response is worth marking because it is not a speech about attitude. He set the people by their families with swords, spears and bows; he arranged for the trumpet to gather them; he told them plainly, our God shall fight for us. Encouragement in Scripture is nearly always concrete — a reordering of the work, a weapon in the hand, a reminder of a specific promise — rather than an appeal to feel differently. And Isaiah 44:26 supplies the promise that answers decay at the root: God says to cities in ruins that they shall be built, and He is described in that same verse as the One who confirms the word of His servant. The decayed places are raised by the word of a God who keeps His word, which is precisely why a man may report his weakness honestly and still refuse the sentence we are not able.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew kashal (H3782), to stumble or totter, of the failing strength; chorbah (H2723), a waste or desolate place, the decayed places God promises to raise.

expand to see more

Hebrew kashal (H3782) — to stumble, to totter, to fail; the strength of the bearers of burdens is decayed; Nehemiah 4:10.

Hebrew chorbah (H2723) — a ruin, a desolation; I will raise up the decayed places thereof; Isaiah 44:26.

Hebrew aphar (H6083) — dust, rubbish; the heaps out of which the wall was rebuilt; Nehemiah 4:2.

Hebrew qum (H6965) — to rise, to raise up, to confirm; God confirms the word of his servant and raises the ruins; Isaiah 44:26.

Greek diaphtheiro (G1311) — to corrupt utterly, to perish; though our outward man perish; 2 Corinthians 4:16.

Usage

"“The strength of the bearers of burdens is decayed” — an honest report."

"“So that we are not able to build the wall” — the sentence that leaves God out."

"“I will raise up the decayed places thereof” — said by the God who confirms His servant's word."
